Thieves break into France’s Renoir Museum, make away with 3 paintings worth millions

Police spotted the thieves and gave chase, during which they dropped one painting but escaped with the other three, he said.

Reuters

08 September, 2026 03:36 pm IST

A sign at the entrance of the Renoir Museum after four paintings were stolen by thieves in an early-morning break-in, with two recovered nearby, in Cagnes-sur-Mer, on the French Riviera, France, September 8, 2026. | Manon Cruz/Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Thieves stole three paintings from the  Renoir  Museum  on the French Riviera early on Tuesday, the local mayor said.

The raiders broke into the  museum  a little before 6 a.m. and took four paintings, Cagnes-sur-Mer mayor Bryan Masson said on his Facebook page.

Police spotted the thieves and gave chase, during which they dropped one painting but escaped with the other three, he said.

Show Full Article

“Attacking the  Renoir  museum  is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer. These actions are particularly serious,” Masson said in his message.

The  museum  was created in 1960 in the mansion of the impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste  Renoir  on a hill in Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, where he died in 1919. The collection on display in the  museum  includes 13 paintings from the master and some 40 sculptures, furniture and photographs.

Masson did not identify the paintings that were stolen.  Renoir ‘s most valuable works have fetched dozens of millions of dollars at auctions in the past.

Art thieves in Europe are committing more violent robberies and specialist gangs have been replaced by ad hoc opportunists recruited through social media, pan-European police body Europol said last month.

The heist at the Louvre  Museum  in Paris in October last year was a prime example of this, Europol said, as the thieves threatened guards and visitors and stole €88 million ($102.3 million) worth of jewels, such as Empress Eugenie’s tiara.

A Hindu group visited the Eiffel Tower to pray. Women told to ‘step aside’

The instructions during a BAPS delegation’s private visit sparked a staff strike and a political backlash in France.

Himanshi Aggarwal

08 September, 2026 10:21 am IST

2

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Swami Keshavvandas, the sixth and current spiritual guru of the BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha, at the Eiffel Tower on Saturday | Photo: @BritIndianVoice/X

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

New Delhi: The Eiffel Tower was closed to the public on Monday after staff staged a strike in protest over the treatment of female employees during a visit by a Hindu religious delegation. Women workers at the site were reportedly asked to leave their workstations or stay out of sight during the visit, according to workers and management.

According to reports, a group of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) was visiting as part of events linked to the inauguration of a new temple near Paris. Union representative Diane Davoine said women were instructed to step aside so male colleagues could take their places as the delegation passed through.

“During the visit of this delegation, women were asked to leave their places of work in order to place men there,” Davoine told Reuters. She also said management had apologised to workers over the incident.

Show Full Article

“So that absolutely does not go down well with the employees, with women obviously, who are all humiliated by what happened, by the way some were treated,” she said.

She added: “Tensions mounted over the weekend, so this morning, the employees decided to meet: first, to open a dialogue with management, and second, to ensure that women are never treated this way at the company again.”

In a statement, staff condemned “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex”. Some workers were reportedly told to withdraw to other areas or avoid certain zones while the group was present. The delegation was accompanied only by male staff on parts of the visit, including the third floor.

The Société d’Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel (SETE), which operates the monument, confirmed that the delegation had requested that the visit be organised to limit “interactions with women”. SETE said those conditions “should not have been accepted” and that management had apologised to staff. SETE president Ariel Weil said the company would investigate and “draw the necessary conclusions”.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire called the arrangement “unacceptable”.

“It is not acceptable that such conditions can be tolerated,” he wrote in a post on X. “These are neither my values, nor those that the Eiffel Tower should uphold, where everyone—regardless of gender—should be able to move about and act freely, without distinction between women and men.”

“I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors,” Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of the National Assembly, wrote in a post on X. “In France, women fully occupy public spaces. No one dictates to them that they must become invisible there.”

The BAPS temple in Paris later issued a statement saying it took the concerns “very seriously”.

“To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower,” the statement read. “Nevertheless, we sincerely apologise for any pain or inconvenience caused.”

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)
